title: Eukaryotic cell ultrastructure; Prokaryotic cells and viruses
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: CE02b#t3 term and clue written for the game; CE04a#t4 term and clue written for the game; CE04b#t1 term and clue written for the game; CE04a#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: CE04a#N.3a, CE04b#N.2a, CE04a#N.12, CE04b#N.5, CE04a#N.13a, CE04b#N.7, CE04b#N.9.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Chitin
items.clue: The substance that fungal walls are made of

items.label: Lysozyme
items.clue: An enzyme that strips away the wall of a bacterium

items.label: Capsid
items.clue: Coat of protein around the genetic material of a virus

items.label: Prokaryotic
items.clue: Describes cells with no nucleus, such as bacteria and archaea

questions.stem: Which description of the structure of a Bacillus cell is correct?

options.text: A loop of naked DNA lies in the cytoplasm, and proteins are made on 70S ribosomes.
The DNA is enclosed by a nuclear membrane inside a small nucleus within the cytoplasm.
The cell wall outside the plasma membrane is built from long parallel fibres of cellulose.
The DNA loop is wound around histone proteins to package it within the nucleoid region.

questions.explanation: A Gram-positive eubacterium such as Bacillus has a cell wall, a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, naked DNA in a loop lying in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm, and 70S ribosomes on which its proteins are synthesised.

questions.stem: Which feature is shared by all viruses?

options.text: A capsid of protein enclosing either DNA or RNA, but not both
A cytoplasm in which the virus carries out metabolism
A membrane of phospholipid forming the outermost layer
A genome of DNA together with RNA, as in any living cell

questions.explanation: The few features common to all viruses are a small, fixed size; nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, as genetic material; a capsid made of protein; no cytoplasm; and few or no enzymes. No virus contains both DNA and RNA as its genetic material.

questions.stem: After Gram staining, a culture of rod-shaped bacteria appears red under the microscope. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: They are Gram-positive bacilli, as their cells have kept the red safranin counterstain.
They are Gram-negative cocci, which have a thin wall surrounded by an outer membrane.
They are Gram-positive bacilli, because their thick peptidoglycan has absorbed the safranin.
They are Gram-negative bacilli; penicillin is likely to be less effective against them.

questions.explanation: Red means the crystal violet was washed out of a thin wall: Gram-negative. Their outer membrane keeps many antibiotics, including penicillin, away from the peptidoglycan.

questions.stem: A newly discovered particle 30 nm across contains one molecule of single-stranded RNA inside a protein shell. It has no ribosomes and it multiplies only inside living cells. How does the particle multiply?

options.text: It grows to about twice its size inside the cell and then divides into two identical particles.
Its RNA and proteins are made by the host cell's machinery and then assembled into new particles.
It absorbs nutrients from the cell into its cytoplasm and metabolises them to build copies of itself.
It must first acquire a DNA molecule, because one RNA strand cannot act as genetic material.

questions.stem: An electron micrograph shows a cell about 3 µm long. It has a cell wall, a paler fibrous region of DNA not enclosed by any membrane, many small dense granules, and no membrane-bound organelles. How should the cell be classified?

options.text: As a plant cell, because a cell wall is found only around the cells of plants.
As a eukaryote, because the region containing DNA must be a nucleus, as every cell has one.
As a prokaryote, because its DNA lies in a nucleoid region and it has no membrane-bound organelles.
As a eukaryote, because prokaryotic cells are too simple to contain any ribosomes.

questions.stem: Bacteriophage lambda does not multiply in a sterile nutrient broth containing amino acids, nucleotides and ATP, but does multiply when living E. coli cells are added to the broth. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The phage's own enzymes and ribosomes work only once they are activated inside a cell's cytoplasm.
The phage lacks ribosomes and most enzymes, so it needs a cell's protein synthesis machinery.
The phage cannot absorb dissolved nutrients from the broth, but it can feed on the contents of a cell.
The phage has to attach to a cell wall before it can grow large enough to divide in two.

questions.stem: A culture of E. coli cells carrying the lambda prophage is growing normally. It is exposed to ultraviolet light, and about an hour later most of the cells lyse and release phages. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The prophage had been releasing phages all along, and the ultraviolet light merely burst the cells.
A prophage cannot cause lysis, so the culture must have been contaminated by a separate lytic phage.
Damage to the host DNA induced the prophage to be excised from the chromosome and enter the lytic cycle.
The ultraviolet light made the prophage grow and divide repeatedly until the cells burst.
